item.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready
item.description:
“We believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”

Welcome to Edition 9.16 of the Rocket Report! Lots of SpaceX-related news this week including a couple of Thursday shockers. In one story, the company told the US Space Force thanks, but no thanks after being offered three military launch contracts. Then, on the civil space side of things, SpaceX’s Starship may required up to 22 refuelings to support a lunar landing, a NASA safety panel said.

As always, wewelcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Miura 5 getting closer to launch. PLD Space says its Miura 5 rocket, due to undertake its inaugural launch next year, is nearing final integration,Aviation Week reports. The rocket is one of three Miura 5s the company has already manufactured, with the other two designed to qualify key system elements, CEO Raúl Torres said in an October 19 program update. PLD Space now targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027.

Fully integrated stage… “Manufacturing these three vehicles has allowed our teams to work continuously across different stages of production and integration, applying the lessons learned from each qualification campaign directly to the launch vehicle,” Torres said. One Miura 5 second stage is now fully integrated to kick off system-level testing under representative operating conditions. The second stage is at PLD’s Teruel test facility for its qualification campaign, including wet dress rehearsal and a static hot-fire test.

Reaction Dynamics seeks to raise $350 million. One of three prominent Canadian launch startups, Reaction Dynamics, said it is seeking to raise $350 million to grow its staff from 68 to more than 350 people,spaceQ reports. The company is developing the small-lift Aurora rocket, which Reaction Dynamics hopes will reach orbit in 2028. Reaction Dynamics also announced plans to build a medium-lift rocket, Borealis, for a debut by 2031.

You’ve got the aurora, and the borealis… With a lift capacity of 6 tons to low-Earth orbit, Borealis would carry a little under half of the advertised payload capacity of Rocket Lab’s Neutron vehicle. “We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” the company’s founder and chief executive, Bachar Elzein, said. “Aurora is how we get to orbit in 2028. Borealis is how we deliver sovereign access to orbit, at scale, by 2031.” Both of the dates appear to be highly aspirational, but we wish them luck.

Rocket Lab sets next Electron launch date. After 97 launches of Electron, it is not exactly news that Rocket Lab is preparing for its 98th launch of the vehicle.The mission, launching three HAWK satellites for the constellation operator HawkEye 360, is due to launch as early as 07:00 UTC on Friday, October 23.

So why are you writing about it? … Two reasons. First of all, it’s worth noting that Rocket Lab continues to be only the second company to develop and frequently fly a purely commercial rocket. Secondly, we love the name of the mission, “We’re Not Hawking Around.” Kudos to the Rocket Lab team for keeping launch fun and fresh, even after moving through dozens of launches.

SpaceX says no thanks to Space Force launches. The Space Force recently tried to book rides for three future satellite missions, but SpaceX declined to offer its services,Politico reports. No other rocket companies offered to take them either, the publication reported. A top Space Force official, Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the acting portfolio acquisition executive, acknowledged growing pains for the government and space industry as demand for rockets increases. “Temporarily, there are some things we’ll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying,” he said. SpaceX has been declining to sign new Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch contracts for all kinds of customers.

No one else has capacity… The three Space Force missions that didn’t find a ride were listed through the National Security Space Launch initiative. Two of the missions were for the Space Development Agency. The agency is a branch of the Space Force that’s building a network of hundreds of military satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide expanded data services, and missile warning and tracking capabilities. Other potential launch providers, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin, are both working through setbacks with their launch vehicles. Zarybnisky remained optimistic that Blue Origin and ULA will work through their technical problems and that new competitors will get up and running in time.

Who will win the medium-lift launch race? It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. Nearly a decade and a half later, there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.

Which comes first… In a new article,Ars updates the statusof four medium-lift rockets under development in the United States: Stoke Space’s Nova, Relativity Space’s Terran R, Rocket Lab’s Neutron, and the Eclipse vehicle being built by Firefly and Northrop Grumman. The publication also (somewhat hazardously) predicts the order in which the four rockets will make their debut.

Japanese rocket launches historic Phobos mission. Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth,Ars reports. The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan.

This has been tried before… The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan’s flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan’s heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. MMX is not the first mission to attempt a sample return from Phobos. Russia’s Phobos-Grunt sample return mission failed soon after launch in 2011, before it could set off for Mars. (submitted by tsunam)

Chinese rocket debris found in Midwest. In September, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest,Ars reports. The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.

A surprising find… The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks.

Arianespace targets Nov. 23 return for Ariane 6. Arianespace has announced that the next Ariane 6 launch will take place no earlier than November 23, marking the rocket’s return to flight after ground testing reportedly revealed an issue with one of its turbopumps,European Spaceflight reports. The flight will carry 36 Amazon Leo satellites aboard an Ariane 64, the rocket’s four-booster configuration. It will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since the rocket’s inaugural flight in July 2024.

Situation is on track… Arianespace’s new announcement follows a report from French newspaper La Tribune, published a day earlier, claiming ArianeGroup had resolved an anomaly affecting a liquid hydrogen turbopump that had disrupted the rocket’s launch schedule. According to the report, the anomaly was first detected during an engine acceptance test shortly before the start of summer. Asked by European Spaceflight to comment on the report, an ArianeGroup spokesperson declined to address it directly and instead pointed to the newly announced launch date. “The next launch has been announced today, so the situation is on track.”

How many Starships will be required for a lunar landing? On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon,Ars reports. One of these is the number of refuelings required to support a Starship lunar landing.

Uncertainty remains… “With respect to Artemis IV, however, we’ve got a large number of firsts that reduce the likelihood of mission success,” Precourt said. “We need to keep our eyes on numerous required fuelings for the lander. I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.” In response to this, SpaceX founder Elon Musk replied that NASA’s safety panel estimate was not accurate. “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.”

SpaceX will attempt a rocket and upper stage catch. It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive Starship rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight,Ars reports. SpaceX founder Elon Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures.

Working with the FAA… Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said.

Blue Origin goes bigger on New Glenn. Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its already considerable Florida launch facilities last Friday with the intent of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year from there,Ars reports. The company said it would add two launch pads for the New Glenn rocket, in addition to two already under construction at Cape Canaveral. The company is also investing heavily in a new manufacturing facility that will produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger variant of the New Glenn rocket.

More missions… The company also plans to procure two additional landing ships to catch and return the first stage of the New Glenn rocket (it currently has one, named Jacklyn). Finally, Blue Origin said it would add a new customer integration facility, built in conjunction with the US Space Force, that will feature four payload bays to process multiple missions at the same time. “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,” said Ian Richardson, senior vice president of operations at Blue Origin.

October 23: Electron | We’re Not Hawking Around | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 07:00 UTC

October 23: Long March 6A | Unknown payload | Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, China | 10:15 UTC

October 23: Long March 4B | Unknown payload | Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, China | 19:25 UTC

item.title: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees
item.description:
Friday the 13thprequel series based on Jason’s mom drags at first, then hits a vein.

Peacock’s series,Crystal Lake, doesn’t feel like aFriday the 13thmovie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the originalFriday the 13thmovie but avoids majorCrystal Lakespoilers.)

Instead,Crystal Lakestrives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son Jason.

Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth.

Ars dug into news archives and found interviews where Palmer explained that the later films did nothing to expand the character, offering only “stupid” lines. There was no reason for the actor—who at the height of her fame dated James Dean and was often typecast as the sweet-faced girl-next-door—to stoop to stepping back into Pam’s shoes. She famously only agreed to do the first movie because her Mercedes broke down on the Connecticut Turnpike and she needed a new car. She worked 10 days to capture her scenes, got paid $10,000, bought a new car, and expected nobody to remember her performance.

“I read that script and thought ‘What a piece of junk,’” Palmer said in 2005.

Palmer often criticized the later movies for bringing back Jason’s mom but giving her nothing to do. So, while some die-hardFriday the 13thfans may findCrystal Lakeslow and foreign in the first few episodes, it’s worth sticking around for the first stab at fulfilling Palmer’s dream of Pam being more than just a helicopter mom of a vengeful boy living at the bottom of a cursed lake.

Crystal Lakeshowrunner Brad Caleb Kane—who previously produced HBO’sWelcome to Derry,whichgave Pennywise from Stephen King’sITa riveting backstory—took many liberties when approaching Pam’s backstory, including shifting the timeline of events.

In the original movie, Jason dies in 1958, but Kane wanted to root the story in historical events that resonated with the themes from the movie, so he shifted Jason’s drowning to 1971–2. Hetold Daily Deadthat it was more important to him to do a “character-rich,” “emotionally resonant” show. By having Jason conceived in the early 1960s, he could draw on actual experiments on mothers during that time and invent a corporate enemy whose experiments on Pam set her up to become the type of fiercely protective mother who would kill for her son. Talkingto Esquire, he explained that “continuity is wonky, anyway” across the movies. And by shifting the timeline, he told the Daily Dead that he got to weave in a scientific “Douglas Sirk-meets-David Cronenberg” body horror episode that you’d never expect would come out of a Friday the 13th franchise installment.

Without spoiling plot details, I’ll note this backstory injects much more tension into the moment that Jason drowns at the camp. It also makes Pam’s desperation to believe that Jason’s still alive—and needs her to kill counselors for his protection—much more relatable. In interviews, Kane confirmed he wanted to add context to key moments in the original movie without feeling bound to perfectly tie in the series.

In interviews, Palmer confirmed that she invented her own backstory for Pam that went back to conception, too. In her version, Pam gets pregnant in high school and decides to have him anyway, which is why she’s so protective of Jason. In 1982, Palmer said that she hoped through her intense acting that viewers would sense that there was more good in Pam than viewers knew, saying, “I can never play a part where I think there’s nothing good about the person at all. You hope that acting can explain why people do some of the things that they do—to show some truth.”

Kane told Daily Dead that when he spoke to Linda Cardellini about portraying Pam inCrystal Lake, she agreed that the character must be played in “protective mama bear mode” because “it all goes back to Jason, her love for Jason, and her dedication to Jason.”

ForFriday the 13thfans who early on might feel impatient forCrystal Laketo stop talking about evil corporations and self-help gurus and get back to the camp slayings they came for, don’t fret, you won’t have to wait that long. By the third episode, murderous Jason begins to more prominently feature in episodes and the gory deaths begin, as a swarm of innocent hippies ignore warnings and are drawn into the camp, like lambs to the slaughter.

This is the turning point when the TV series starts to feel more familiar and picks up the pace measurably. Although the hockey mask never appears, Kane lovingly re-creates exact scenes from the original movie to offer flashes of eye candy to Jason fanatics. There are easter eggs all over, and the series offers a good excuse to rewatch the original movie to catch even more and compare the gorgeous haunting lake views.

Kane is hoping that the series finally showing the horrifying but oddly relatable depth of this unshakeable connection between mother and son will be a hit, so it can possibly run for multiple seasons, he told Esquire.

When pitching the series to A24, Kane knew he wanted to do his own thing, while maintaining that “what was sacred to me is that a certain segment of the fans feel like I was doing a loving homage to the movies,” he told Daily Dead. On this mission, the series weaves in town folk names and lines from the original movie, as well as, of course, bringing back Pam Voorhees’ iconic cable-knit sweater. The series also seems to nod to Palmer’s past in making Cardellini’s Pam a well-known singer who styles her hair similarly to how young Palmer did in her starlet days.

Growing up the kind of kid who read novelizations of horror movies, Kane also made sure that the special effects makeup is next-level. He worked with “very detail-oriented” artists who leave little to the imagination, as hippie numbers dwindle, eyes are gouged, and mother and son “go fullFriday the 13th” by the series end.

item.title: Ukraine learns to fight without Starlink as Musk plays politics with satellites
item.description:
Ukraine has changed drone and war-fighting tech to reduce reliance on Starlink.

Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it.

As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. This has enabled Ukraine tomaintain vital communicationsfor both civilian purposes and military operations—and has also expanded the Ukrainian military’s capability to remotely control or provide guidance to drones used in both air defense against Russian attacks and for striking back at Russian targets.

“Starlink currently offers some of the best satellite coverage available, with virtually no competitors when you consider the combination of cost, availability, and ease of use,” according to the head of hardware R&D at the Ukrainian defense companyBlueBird Tech, who provided comments to Ars anonymously for security reasons. “In practical terms, the main limitation is the need to position the antenna so it can receive signals from the satellites.”

The US government and European countries such as Poland andGermany have paid SpaceXfor tens of thousands of commercial Starlink terminals to be sent to Ukraine, as well as covering subscription fees. The US government has also given Ukraine’s military access to a military-grade version of Starlink known as Starshield, which Ukrainian defense companies can also test in their technologies in cooperation with the military, according to the BlueBird Tech representative.

Starlink terminals have also been deployed onUkrainian ground robotsanddrone boatsoperating in the contested Black Sea, in addition to supporting many differentaerial drone operationson the battlefield. But even before the latest Starlink disruptions began on October 13, Ukrainian companies and their Western partners had already begun deploying more drones that reduce or eliminate communications reliance on Starlink.

The Starlink service provided by Musk’s company SpaceX has proven so invaluable to modern battlefield operations that even Russian military units were using smuggled Starlink terminals—at least beforeSpaceX shut off accessto any Starlink terminal within Ukraine not on a whitelist in February 2026. That shutoff severely disrupted Russian battlefield operations in the early part of the year.

But access to Starlink has become a double-edged sword for Ukraine as well. Early warning signs arose in February 2023, when SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell confirmed reports that Musk’s company was taking steps toblock Ukraine’s military from using Starlink with drones. That followed Musk’s social media comments about not allowing Starlink to be used for “long-range drone strikes.”

The top-down Starlink restrictions returned on October 13, 2026, when Ukrainian government officials and military forces reported that the military-gradeStarlink service was being throttledfor terminals exceeding speeds of about 99 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). This latest restriction wasimposed by SpaceX reportedly at Musk’s orderand potentially in consultation with President Donald Trump. Musk and the Trump administration have both denied responsibility while pointing fingers at each other.

In practice, the throttling of Starlink in Ukraine has made the satellite service unstable at even lower speeds like 80 miles per hour (130 kilometers per hour), saidMichael Kofman, a senior fellow in the Russia and Eurasia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, in asocial media poston October 19.

Such throttling reportedly disrupted multiple Ukrainian drone missions when it began without warning in the middle of the night. Ukrainian officials and advisers have described multiple impacts on drones that supply frontline units, reconnaissance missions, andmid-range drone strike missionsthat attack Russian military units and supply lines in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

The new Starlink speed limits have even reportedly interfered with Ukraine’s air defenses that use fast-moving drone interceptors to take down Russian one-way attack drones,according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Starlink disruptioncoincided with some of Russia’s largest drone and missile attacks yeton major Ukrainian cities, with Russia having stepped up targeting of Ukraine’s power grid,data centersand even blocks of residential apartment buildings.

Despite the value of Starlink, Ukraine’s military and defense companies have already been figuring out ways to fight on without the satellite service. This is in part because Russian forces have done their best to interfere with Starlink signals on the battlefield, including recentlydeploying cumbersome jamming systemsto create zones of disrupted service within the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

“We don’t tie our products to any single technology, and we don’t manufacture systems that are critically dependent on Starlink,” the BlueBird Tech representative told Ars. “We’ve long been aware of the risks of Starlink jamming along the front line, which is why we’ve avoided using it as the sole means of control and telemetry.”

BlueBird Tech has integrated Starlink terminals in several of its ground-based and airborne systems, but its representative described this as a “small percentage” of its overallproduct lineup. For example, the company’s Zhakh FPV drones are among the many Ukrainian and Russian drones that can maintain physical communication links with human operators by unspooling a long fiber-optic cable—making them impervious to electronic warfare countermeasures.

The Ukrainian company produces multiple types of drones for reconnaissance and strike missions, along with a ground robot, drone detection systems, and electronic warfare systems. It has also begundeveloping an air-defense interceptor drone.

There are still “certain product configurations for which no direct replacement for Starlink currently exists,” because the satellite service’s “technical capabilities and accessibility make it difficult to substitute in some applications,” the BlueBird Tech representative said. But they also described the company as “actively exploring ways to add redundancy and potentially replace these components in the future.”

Some of the most promising wireless approaches include using ground-based LTE or 5G wireless networks or even turning to laser-based optical communication.

BlueBird Tech is also examining radio-based mesh networks that allow ground transmitters or even radio-equipped drones to act as relay nodes within a larger decentralized communications system. This approach has been increasingly implemented by Russian drone strike missions on Ukrainian cities, as detailed byThe Kyiv Independent.

Another Ukrainian defense company, Buntar Aerospace, described having always accounted for the possibility that a communications service like Starlink could become available because of battlefield conditions.

“The recent Starlink and Starshield disruptions did not affect our operations because we had prepared for this scenario in advance,” saidBohdan Sas, cofounder of Buntar Aerospace, in an email to Ars. “Losing access to one communications service does not necessarily mean losing the ability to conduct a mission.”

Buntar Aerospace has provided Ukrainian military forces with fixed-wing reconnaissance drones that can fly up to 62 miles (100 kilometers). The drone’s operations benefit from AI-driven software called Buntar Copilot that can supposedly adapt flight plans for factors such as weather, signal quality or interference, and battery life.

The companydescribes each data stream from its Buntar-3 drone—such as flight sensor data or its camera video stream—as being transmitted over separate channels to reduce the impact of one dropped stream. Although the droneincorporates a Starlink terminal, it also has alternative communication methods in case any service is disrupted.

“Commercial communications services can provide valuable capabilities, but defense systems must account for the possibility that those services may become unavailable,” Sas told Ars.

Western companies providing drone technologies to Ukraine have also incorporated similar battlefield lessons to reduce reliance on Starlink. For example, German defense company Quantum Systems described its Vector reconnaissance drones deployed in Ukraine as able to communicate with ground control stations via encrypted radio links. It also has “onboard AI and alternative navigation technologies” to perform missions despiteGPS jammingor electronic warfare measures.

The SPYS drone interceptor—developed by the company’s German-Ukrainian joint venture Quantum WIY Industries—also uses a ground-based beacon system to navigate without GPS and has AI-based target recognition capabilities coupled with heat-seeking sensors to home in on enemy drones. This particular interceptor does not use Starlink at all.

“As a global neo-prime with European roots, we want Europe to remain fully capable of operating alongside our allies while retaining the ability to act independently when necessary,” said Paul Strobel, a spokesperson for German defense company Quantum Systems, in an email to Ars. “This means Europe must be able to develop, operate and maintain critical technologies, data and capabilities independently.”

The German government hasprovided fundingto supply tens of thousands of these interceptor drones to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027.

Given their governments’ funding for Starlink service in Ukraine, German and Polish leaders havedemanded that the Starlink restrictions be removedandasked pointed questionsabout whether Musk is “playing politics.” But Europe has also been accelerating development of its own sovereign alternatives to Starlink that may prove useful for Ukraine in the future.

The Ukrainians already use Eutelsat’s OneWeb satellite service as a main alternative for some communications, butEutelsat has just over 600 satellites in orbitcompared toStarlink’s 10,000 satellites. This means it cannot support nearly as much data streaming or as many customers for Ukraine or other regions.

The OneWeb terminals are also significantly bigger than Starlink terminals while costing about 45 times more than the latter,The Economist reported. Caleb Henry, author of a book about the history of OneWeb, previously told Ars that the bulkier OneWeb terminalscomplicated Ukrainian efforts to mount them on drones.

The European Union has already spent six yearsplanning to launch the IRIS² constellationof348 communications satellitesstarting in 2029, although that is again a mere fraction of the Starlink constellation’s size. European Union leaders have also been seeking to speed up antitrust approval for a satellite venture called Project Bromo, which could create a large European company to rival SpaceX,Bloomberg Newsreported.

Separately, Germany plans to build its own communications satellite constellation, SATCOMBw 4, for its own military and NATO. This constellation aims to start with 50 operational satellites by 2029 before expanding to hundreds,according to Euronews.

Just weeks before the latest Starlink disruptions in Ukraine,Finland’s satellite company ICEYEand communications technology firm Nokia also announced plans to build a communications satellite constellation for Europe, according toBloomberg News. The companies expect to launch up to 50 low-Earth orbit satellites annually from 2028 onward.

But as with Starlink, enemy countermeasures could also disrupt signals from these communications satellite services on modern battlefields. So Ukrainian defense companies and the military will likely keep backup systems and avoid overreliance on satellite signals whenever possible.

“The main lesson is that communications resilience is part of military autonomy,” said Sas at Buntar Aerospace. “Defense technologies must be designed around the realities of the battlefield, where connectivity is never guaranteed.”

item.title: The reactor meant to showcase nuclear’s comeback keeps hitting problems
item.description:
A contractor fell into a reactor cavity and a bundle of fuel rods almost fell over.

US regulators have issued a warning to a nuclear project critical to Donald Trump’s efforts to revive the industry, after a contractor fell into a reactor cavity and a bundle of fuel rods nearly tipped over during refuelling.

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission told Holtec International, a company racing to reopen a shuttered reactor at the Palisades nuclear power plant in Michigan, to address a “chilled work environment” that has made staff hesitant to raise safety concerns without fear of retaliation.

The warning has prompted concerns among critics that financial and political pressures to revitalise nuclear power as an answer to booming AI-driven energy demand are increasing risks of accidents.

The NRC performed an inspection at Palisades in July over concerns about safety awareness. It followed an incident last year in which a worker fell into the reactor cavity, ingested some water and was sent off-site for medical attention. The individual was decontaminated by radiation protection personnel but had 300 counts per minute detected in their hair, according to an incident report.

In a second incident in August, a bundle of nuclear fuel rods tilted over during a refuelling operation, delaying what was anticipated to be the first reopening of a shuttered nuclear reactor in the US.

The NRC also said nine of the 15 reactor operators at Palisades failed the test for an initial licence examination administered in July and August. Six individuals were issued operator licences.

Holtec, which has never operated a nuclear power plant, has secured about $2.2 billion in government support for a project that has been touted as a symbol of US nuclear resurgence. The owners of two other nuclear plants slated for decommissioning—Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania and Duane Arnold in Iowa—announced restarts soon after Palisades began work.

The Trump administration has promoted nuclear energy as an edge in the AI race against China. It has slashed regulation, provided tens of billions of dollars in funds and promised to reverse a culture of “risk aversion” at the NRC to accelerate projects.

The warning issued to Holtec by the NRC last week landed as investor interest in the nuclear sector has faded, driven by concerns the AI boom is slowing.

More than $30 billion has been wiped off the value of five of the largest US-listed nuclear energy companies in the last year—Oklo, Centrus Energy, BWX Technologies, NuScale and Nano Nuclear. Last month, Holtec was forced to postpone a planned initial public offering that was expected to raise $900 million and value the New Jersey-based company at up to $10 billion.

Palisades first became operational in 1971. It was decommissioned in 2022 but received a $1.5 billion loan from the Department of Energy in 2024 to finance its restoration.

“The situation at Palisades is that you have a power plant operator newbie in Holtec trying to restart a nuclear reactor, and they may be under a lot of financial and political pressure to get this done speedily,” said Allison Macfarlane, who served as NRC chair from 2012 to 2014.

“The ‘chilled work environment’ warning issued by the NRC raises concerns that staff don’t feel like they can speak up to raise safety concerns and prevent accidents,” she added. “That perhaps reflects the new culture sweeping through part of the industry—move fast and break things. But to ensure safety, nuclear needs a culture based on going slowly and carefully.”

Holtec faces a March 2027 contractual deadline to begin supplying power to customers, who secured an extra $1.3 billion in government funds to buy power from Palisades.

In a statement to the FT, Holtec said it took the issues identified by the NRC seriously and was addressing them to ensure the plant runs safely. It said the fuel assembly that tilted over was successfully recovered without spilling in a “remarkable demonstration of technical ingenuity.”

“A strong safety-conscious work environment is fundamental to our culture,” the company said. “The assertion that we have rushed has directly been countered by the work that has been accomplished.”

The NRC told Holtec its concerns about workplace culture must be addressed promptly to prevent further “cultural decline” within the affected departments. NRC has asked Holtec to correct the problems and will review the company’s plan within 30 days.

However, the NRC downplayed any immediate risk to the public, saying mitigating measures ensured plant safety was not compromised. Holtec said the worker who fell into the reactor cavity last year had sustained minor injuries from the fall but quickly returned to work.

Holtec, which is trying to transform itself from a supplier of nuclear components and services into a reactor design and plant operator, has faced governance questions in the past. It has been the target of a whistleblower lawsuit and legal disputes involving former executives, relating to allegations of financial misrepresentation, executive retaliation and fraudulent practices.

Kris Singh, founder and chief executive of Holtec, rejected the claims in a prior interview with the FT.

item.title: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said “HLX” in public
item.description:
Sound designer lets Half Life-related codename slip at a conference.

Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up toHalf-Life 2(afterso, so many years) may remember last year’sflurryofspeculationthatHalf-Life 3wasfinally nearing completion. Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development.

That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel atGameSoundCon, an industry conference devoted to “the art, technology, and business of game audio.” In a panel devoted to Valve’s use of open audio engines (captured inthis Vimeo clip), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio:

Our HDR system is basically that’s one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR.HLX has its own version, so on and so forth [emphasis added].

“HLX,” of course, has beenwidely reportedas the internal code name for Valve’s next Half-Life project. The codename has shown upin Valve engine code since at least 2024, but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Moraskywas responsible for a close callin an interview last year).

In the panel video, fellow panelist and Valve sound designer David Feise can be seen mumbling a sarcastic “nice work” to Morasky after the HLX codename slips out of his mouth. Later, while the audience is clapping at the end of the Q&A session, Feise leans in to Morasky and appears to say, “Good job—you only said HLX once!”

An official utterance of the “HLX” shibboleth is of course a good sign for those looking for any indication of the franchise continuing beyond 2020’sHalf-Life Alyx. But the question of when Valve will make its next Half-Life project official still looms large.

Remember, it was just under a year ago that journalist Mike Straw wasadamant thatHalf-Life 3would be a Steam Machine launch title. Now that the Steam Machine launchhas come and gonewithout even a nod toward an announcement, we can understand why Valve watchers would be more gun-shy than usual over any new rumors.

Longtime Valve watcher Tyler McVicker—whosaidHalf-Life 3was in the “final stages of development”andsuggested a 2026 announcement was “likely”last year—admitted ina recent videothat he now doesn’t believe that HLX is being announced this calendar year. But he also pointed to recently increased coding activity within Valve (as measured by externally viewable internal “commit” numbers) that something big might be coming sooner than later.

One thing is for sure: WheneverHalf-Life 3finally is announced and released, it will have to be truly incredible to make up for the loss of thelong-runningmetagameofspeculatingaboutits mere existence.

item.title: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report
item.description:
Corporate phishing tests are common, but this one was especially cruel.

The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email promising free championship rings in a test of its staff’s ability to detect scams, The New York Timesreportedyesterday. “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” the email sent in late September said, instructing employees to click a link to make a selection from two ring designs.

Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link “were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns,” the report said, citing team sources. Dolan is the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden.

It’s common for corporations to send phishing emails to find out which employees don’t pay attention to clues that an email is a scam. A cybersecurity-test email often appears to be from the company itself but includes telltale signs of phishing. For example, Ars Technica owner Condé Nast sends phishing-test messages from email addresses with a misspelled domain, “condenest.com.”

It’s not difficult for the typical Ars Technica reporter or editor to spot this kind of tell, but we haven’t received any offer as valuable as a free NBA championship ring. We can hardly blame a Knicks organization staffer for being fooled or at leastgreatly annoyedby a fake offer of a ring commemorating the basketball franchise’s first NBA championship in more than half a century.

The offer wasn’t implausible, either. “Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive,” wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization.

Vardon’s article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.

“Ring orders, designs, and measurements can take time, and not every coaching staff for every defending champion gets its rings on ring night… The Knicks assistants were told they would receive championship rings eventually, but many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks’ business operations, will not receive rings at all, team sources told The Athletic,” Vardon wrote.

MSG employee hopes were raised “at the end of September when the Knicks sent an email to a long list of employees, which gave recipients a first glimpse at their would-be championship rings,” Vardon wrote. The email included “a graphic of two differently styled rings” that the lucky employees could supposedly choose from, the article said.

“(Employee name), this one is on the house. MSG is issuing a complimentary employee championship ring. The same jeweler, the same craftsmanship, personalized with your name. No cost to you,” the email said. “There are two designs to choose from: Championship Gold and Garden Classic. Reserve the one you want below.”

Vardon wrote that “multiple team sources” confirmed the email was a phishing test. It’s not clear how many employees clicked the link or whether any of the employees who received the email will eventually get some type of championship ring. We contacted the Madison Square Garden Sports organization with these questions and will update this article if we get a response.

item.title: RFK Jr.’s vaccine injury clinic could damage NIH hospital, board warns
item.description:
“Trust is slow to build and quick to lose,” board chair Jack Leslie said.

Ata recent meetingof the board that oversees the National Institutes of Health’s Clinical Center Research Hospital, chair Jack Leslie opened with cheerful introductions and gregarious chatter—then diverted from the agenda of the regularly scheduled meeting. He spent the next six minutes delivering a pointed rebuke of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, warning that his anti-vaccine activities could tarnish the venerable hospital, often called the “house of hope” for patients with rare conditions or those who have exhausted all other options.

Leslie took issue with a recent stunt Kennedy had pulled at the hospital, which involved making a surprise appearance for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to open hissignature vaccine injury clinic. The ceremony included a panel with people claiming to have been injured by vaccines. They sat behind placards reading “vaccine injured” and spoke with Kennedy and other high-ranking Trump administration officials.

Leslie prefaced his comments by noting that some might prefer he not speak out against Kennedy’s efforts. “But I think that that would be a failing as an advisory board if we were silent,” he said. Leslie also noted that he has no concerns about studying potential injuries from vaccines. “Serious reactions are rare, but real,” he said, and people who believe they’ve been injured should “be taken seriously.”

In fact, the NIH already has a center that studies vaccine injuries, and Kennedy’s splashy new clinic does not come with more funding or clinic space. The hospital’s CEO,Jonathan Green, who sat next to Leslie at the meeting, chimed in to confirm that “the NIH has conducted research on the safety and efficacy of vaccines for decades in the past, and it ongoes.” Green described Kennedy’s vaccine injury clinic as merely a new, individual “protocol” for the hospital.

“The space in which this protocol will be conducted, the vaccine evaluation center inside the clinical center, has been in existence for decades,” Green said. Like all protocols, it needs to undergo rigorous scientific and ethical reviews before it’s implemented at the hospital. Green said the protocol is still under review.

None of this was made clear in Kennedy’s ceremony, and Leslie condemned the optics of the event, particularly the signs labeling patients “vaccine injured.” Those patients “must come first,” Leslie said. “They deserve our care and respect and they deserve answers.” But Kennedy does them—and the hospital—a disservice, Leslie argued.

“The secretary has spent two decades arguing that vaccines are dangerous,” Leslie said. “Those signs announce the conclusion that the research has not yet reached and that the research exists to test. Think about what that means for those patients. If this research finds evidence of harm, many will dismiss it as the work of a secretary who has long argued that vaccines are dangerous. If it finds none, patients will be told that the clinic was a sham. Either way, they’re left with answers no one trusts, and science only helps patients when the public believes it.”

Leslie said he feared that the stunt sends a political message that will undermine trust that the hospital has worked to earn and maintain for over 70 years.

“The clinical center standing rests on one thing: the confidence of patients, physicians, and the public that the research done here is designed to find the truth, not to confirm a conclusion reached in advance,” he said. “Trust is slow to build and quick to lose. If people come to believe that research at this hospital can be steered toward a politically desired answer, the damage will not stop at vaccines.”

After Leslie’s statement, another member thanked him and made a motion for the board to support the statement. The motion was quickly seconded and, in a voice vote, the board unanimously endorsed the comments.

item.title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs
item.description:
Company says foreign-made robotic vehicles are crucial to US chip production.

US chip champion Intel was so confused by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.” The tech company wanted to make sure that it could continue using certain robotic vehicles in its US chip fabs.

The uncertainty surrounding the Federal Communications Commission ban on certain foreign-made robots was revealed in the agency’s decision to grant Intel’s waiver request. On October 22, theFCC published its orderallowing Intel to continue using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for a period of one year.

The robots in question areautomated guided vehiclesoperating on “tracks or predefined paths” while often requiring operator oversight, according to Intel’s website. They help to move materials and items around within warehouses and factory floors.

Such robotic vehicles are typically manufactured by Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., according toBloomberg News. But the exact types of robotic vehicles used by Intel were only identified in a “confidential appendix” that accompanied its request.

The FCC’s ban mainly covers new models of mobile robots, likehumanoid robotsand robot vacuums, and still allows for the import of robots previously approved for sale in the United States. But theagency rulesseem to restrict major modifications to “previously authorized devices.”

Intel’s waiver request stated that it was “unclear” whether its robotic vehicles even qualify as robots covered by the FCC ban but said it sought relief just in case. The tech company also received approval to “make certain hardware, software, and firmware changes” that would help ensure the continued operation and maintenance of the robotic vehicles.

The tech company described the robotic vehicles as being “critical to its domestic semiconductor manufacturing operations” and argued that the ability to maintain the robots was crucial to avoiding any disruptions to chip production. It also said there are no US-made alternatives that meet the company’s requirements.

The FCC approval came within a week of when Intel filed its waiver request on October 16. That is not too surprising given the importance of Intel to the Trump administration’s plans for reshoring chip manufacturing—not to mention that the US government took an$8.9 billion equity stakein the chip company.

Meanwhile, the US robotics industry at large is still grappling with theconsequences of the FCC ban on foreign-made robots, given that China is the world’s leading supplier of robots and robotic components. Ars previously talked with oneUS robotics distributor that has pivotedfrom importingChina’s humanoid robotsto opening a US manufacturing facility for robots.

Some analysts have warned that the US government’s attempt to boost domestic production of robots via the restrictions on foreign-made robots could backfire for US industry. A report by the market intelligence firmInternational Data Corporationlooks forward to 2030 and estimates that the FCC rule could reduce US revenue from deploying humanoid robots by 58 percent compared to pre-restriction expectations.

item.title: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
item.description:
Birds’ compact nervous system seems to help them handle tasks very quickly.

Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision.

But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions.

“This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?”

To find out, Nieder and his colleague Philipp Schmidbauer put two carrion crows through the same task the monkeys faced, recording their brain activity along the way. The crows solved the task the same way primates do, using the same mathematical logic despite having a very different brain structure. And they did it two times faster.

Nieder and Schmidbauer put two hand-raised crows in front of a touch-sensitive monitor showing a cloud of white dots on black, with some fraction of them drifting coherently left or right or up or down. The birds’ job was to report the overall direction by pecking one of the targets that flanked the display. Correct answers earned them a mealworm.

“We intentionally wanted to have exactly the same random-dot motion task,” Nieder said. “The only difference was that the crows had to peck to indicate their decision, whereas monkeys were indicating by making an eye movement.”

The researchers varied how many dots moved together, ranging from 81 percent of the dots coherently moving together, which is trivially easy to determine, down to 3 percent, which is barely distinguishable from noise. They also included a zero percent condition, in which there was no correct answer.

Both birds scored better than chance, even when only three percent of the dots were moving.

While the crows worked at the task, the team recorded from 248 neurons in the NCL (nidopallium caudolaterale)—a region at the top of the avian processing hierarchy that is widely regarded as the functional counterpart of the primate prefrontal cortex, despite being built differently.

Birds and mammals parted evolutionary ways more than 360 million years ago, and bird brains evolved a different architecture. The mammalian cortex is arranged as stacked sheets of cells, while the equivalent tissue in a bird is organized into dense clusters, with no layering at all. This alternative architecture, Nieder’s study found, proved faster.

Measured from the moment that the dots appeared to the moment the bird’s head started turning to peck at the button, the crows averaged 235 milliseconds. In closely matched versions of the task, monkeys took roughly 410, 490, and 600 milliseconds in three studies. The obvious question was whether the birds simply sacrificed accuracy for speed, but it turned out they did not.

“This would be a simple explanation, that they are very fast at the cost of precision. But that’s not what’s happening,” Nieder said. Crows were as good as monkeys or humans in the same task.

“We’ve never forced the crows to be as quick as possible,” Nieder explained. “We just gave them a self-paced decision. And even in this situation, they were twice as fast compared to any monkey or human that I’m aware of.”

One possible reason for the crows’ speed was that their’ brains were working on a fixed deadline, and the data initially seemed to support that. In primates, difficulty has a large effect on how long a decision takes. In the crows, reaction times ran from 220 milliseconds at the easiest task to just 254 at the hardest, a difference of only 34 milliseconds. But Nieder doesn’t think this means an avian brain is just wired to produce answers on a timer.

“If you zoom in, there is a statistical increase in the reaction time when the coherence is going down,” Nieder said. “They show the same effect as mammals. It’s just much less pronounced, because everything happens much faster.”

There are no shortcuts, he explained, as the crows had to look at the direction of dots’ movement and process this information—they didn’t have any other cues. “That’s why I think they do accumulate evidence. They have to,” Nieder said.

The recordings of neuronal activity show the evidence accumulation in action. Just under a quarter of the neurons sampled, 58 of 248, fired differently depending on which direction the bird would eventually choose, and these neurons started registering that decision incredibly early—about 70 milliseconds after the dots appeared and roughly 170 milliseconds before the bird’s head moved. “The neurons were accumulating sensory evidence, which is very reminiscent of what monkey neurons would do in the neocortex,” Nieder said.

This kind of signal in the brain is called a decision variable, a running tally of evidence that can climb toward a commitment. “It turns out that what we find in the crow brain looks basically the same,” Nieder said. “And that’s interesting considering their brains have evolved very distinctly, as if evolution has found the same physiological mechanism twice, independently.”

So far, the team can’t attribute the crows’ speed to any one particularly fast process. Nieder’s leading explanation is that nearly every biological process runs faster in birds than in mammals.

“We cannot really point our finger to one specific process that is totally faster. It is probably a cascade of different processes that are faster,” Nieder explained. This cascade, he said, begins with vision, since avian visual systems are exquisitely movement-sensitive. It continues through the decision itself and extends to the motor response. Nieder argues there are likely two physiological aspects that make this possible.

The first is simply size. Flight imposes strict weight limits, so birds pack enormous numbers of very small neurons into very small brains. Their axons, the long cable-like fibers that transmit electrical and chemical signals between cells, are shorter.

“Long lines take time. Short lines speed everything up,” Nieder said.

The second factor is temperature. Humans’ body temperature is about 36.6° Celsius, while birds go up to 41, or even 42°. This higher body temperature speeds up all chemical processes in birds’ bodies.

“Every ion channel would open and close faster. Every transmitter would move through the synaptic cleft faster,” Nieder explained. “Evolution really took their bodies to the limit. This is life in the fast lane, not only in the brain, but also respiration, the cardiovascular system—everything is going toward the limit in birds.”

But calling crows (or birds in general) decision-making speed demons comes with a few caveats.

First, the study included only two birds, a rather small sample. “On the one hand, that’s a valid constraint,” Nieder said. “On the other hand, when you look at monkey studies, that’s the standard number of animals that we have for these very complex types of studies, combining behavior and electrophysiology.”

Also, the decision-making time of 235 milliseconds in crows and above 400 milliseconds in primates is not an absolute limit. These times apply to the random dot-motion task, which inherently requires waiting to see which way things are drifting.

Finally, it might be hard to learn whether the results extend beyond corvids or crows specifically. “The problem with many other birds is that they are not as smart as corvids and crows and you need a smart bird in order to train it to do exactly this task,” Nieder said.

So far, he admitted, we can’t be sure whether excellent decision-making skills of crows in his lab are due to birds’ brains being speedy in general or to crows simply being smarter than other avians. “Among birds, the corvids are renowned to be extremely intelligent, so maybe there’s something special about them,” Nieder said.

Science, 2026.  DOI:10.1126/science.aed6459
